utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, let's have Dr. Allcock.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Incidentally, the reason I have advanced another witness, possibly, in place of Damon was because of the non-availability of the witness I told you about who was on and off right up until Friday afternoon, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we ought to be in open session now. Dr. Allcock, thank you for coming back. You are, of course, under the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't know whether the witness does know by any means what the attitude of the Defence is, but he's still at the moment under cross-examination, and it's for them to make their position clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No further cross-examination? Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can the witness please have four exhibits, 1669, 1670, 1671, and 1673. May the witness have copies as well, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you look at 1669 first, please, a reference book bulletin? It's not that one; it's another document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes, right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is something called "Reference Books Bulletin." Just tell us what that is, if you can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I understand that it's a journal that circulates principally among librarians which evaluates the material which is likely to be coming their way and specialises in reference books rather than publications more generally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And that speaks of the conflict in Yugoslavia which I have in my hand and which is available --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- but it says of that, which is a book edited by you and others, that it's "an outstanding reference resource in which a wide array of entries deepen our knowledge of a vital contemporary issue." It goes on to deal with how the book is arranged, and is praiseworthy of it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It does indeed. I was very gratified to see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next document, 1670. Can you tell us from where this comes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, this is the material prepared by the publisher of my forthcoming book. Incidentally, that is already somewhat out of date, in that the publisher has arranged for a joint publication with Columbia University Press, so that that's the publisher's preliminary notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the notice speaks of your book, "Explaining Yugoslavia": "Contradictory images are often presented to us of the lands which were once Yugoslavia. Nothing ever changes," and so on. Next paragraph: "The central claim of this book is that substantial historical discontinuities can be documented in the history of the Balkans, but these are not those captured by reference to age-old hatreds, revolution, nor the clash of civilisations. The patterns of continuity revealed by sociological theory are processes of modernisation and globalisation, and the region is involved in the same processes of development upon which we ourselves are embarked."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We ask you to slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The third document, I have to ask you for what it is, because --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How is this numbered?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 1671; do you have that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, what 1671 is? Because you having been a witness, we haven't been able to talk to you, and it may be I'll withdraw it, but can you tell us what it is before I withdraw it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In the process of producing a substantial academic work, it's quite normal for authors to circulate copies of their material to respected and appropriately qualified colleagues for comment before publication. Naturally the publishers do this, but we also do this independently, on our own initiative. And I sent -- this refers, in fact, it's a response to the text of the book which has already been drawn to your attention, "Explaining Yugoslavia." I sent a copy of that to one of the members of the staff of the American University in Bulgaria, Professor Ivelin Sardamov, for his comment, and the e-mail message which you have in front of you consists of part of his critical response to my text. The reason it's only a part of his response, incidentally, is that the later part of it got into fairly protracted discussion of one particular point of detail, and it didn't seem to me to be particularly relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If anybody wants it, you are prepared to provide it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, again, that's a very flattering review.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not going to read these out in detail, for want of time. If the doctor's credentials come to be put in issue at a later stage, we can look at them then in more detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Incidentally, I'm being pressed to ask you just to tell us that the review we looked at before, that's 1670, which begins, "This is a remarkable book," was reviewed by somebody called Djilas. Who is he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Djilas. Aleksa Djilas is a well-known political scientist. He is actually the son of Milovan Djilas, a well-known politician and dissident in the former Yugoslavia, but who has since made a career for himself as an academic specialist on the region. He is the author of at least three very substantial historical studies of the former Yugoslavia, and my text was sent to him by the publisher as an independent reviewer of the kind to which I've already referred.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The last document, 1673, is simply three pages to remind the Court of what the original exhibit, the book, is and amounts to, "Conflict in the Former Yugoslavia," which we have already seen a review, and includes a forward by Martin Bell.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could I just make one extremely brief comment on that, to the extent that the hardback edition of that work sold out within three months. It's obviously been quite well received.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were asked a number of questions about your expertise and experience, with various comments on tourism as a subject, and observations as to whether you were doing it while you were travelling around the country. Is tourism a serious subject for study? How does it rank as an event in the world, or as a business or an industry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's extremely important. I've heard it said that tourism is now the world's largest industry in terms of the number of people it employs. It certainly is one of the largest aspects of international trade. It's certainly taken seriously by all academic disciplines. I, myself, participate in a study group of the International Sociological Association, which is devoted to the study of tourism, and you'd find similar study groups in organisations of economists or other social scientists.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were then asked a number of questions about sociology and the range of topics that sociology covers or can cover. Is there anything unusual or overbroad about the range of topics that you, in your history as a sociologist, have had to cover? Or is that par for the course?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I'm slightly broader than most sociologists in my coverage. I do remember the previous encounter that ranged over that material, and it struck me that there was an acute confusion underlying part of that questioning between specific areas of sociological expertise, general concepts that might be expected to be the stock in trade of any sociologist and adjacent disciplines. As I think I mentioned on that occasion, I have had to range fairly widely in my work over Yugoslavia because there are so few social scientists, and in particular so few sociologists, who have taken an interest in the area. But I don't think that, bearing in mind that we're talking about a career of 30 years here, that I've been particularly promiscuous in my academic attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Which leads me to my second-to-last question, or my last question before I come to one last short topic. The last question is this: In the field in which you are dealing, are there those whose specialisation, if they are specialists, is much more narrowly focused, or is the body of people dealing with this topic qualified broadly in the areas in which you are qualified? Help us on that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Individuals do vary enormously in how they construct their own specialism. I can think, for example, of a colleague in Britain, Saul Estrin, whose focus is very narrowly econometric, and at the other extreme you would find somebody like the American specialist, Denison Rusinow, who I suppose you would say his range of interest is as broad as my own. Individuals do have to carve out their own academic careers and do so on the basis of a variety of opportunities. I think that perhaps I tend to the broad end of the spectrum because the British academic community, unlike the American academic community, is rather smaller, and therefore, in order to serve the range of interests, both at the teaching and research level, we tend to have to be a little bit more generous in our attentions than our American colleagues, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you said accepted when Judge Bennouna asked you whether you were a generalist, that in the way that that discussion was being explored, that you were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, I think that's fair enough, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Does that in any way invalidate, in your judgement, the ability of you or anybody similarly qualified to express an opinion on these topics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I think it's important to realise that social science, as with all the sciences, there are different functions involved. There are those whose primary task is to advance our knowledge on quite specific points and who legitimately make a career pursuing a really rather narrowly focused range of issues. There is also, within any discipline, an important function to be served by those who are able to synthesise the work of colleagues who choose to take that more focused approach. That's an important component of the discipline, that synthesising function. I have seen my role, in large measure, as -- although not exclusively -- as working in that generalising mode. Certainly recently, when I was working on tourism and agriculture, I was contributing rather more in the specialised mode.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Last topic. You were asked about racism by Mr. Stein raising with you whether that was something that you covered, and I want to deal with one issue of racism with you, please. Will you take your report at Appendix 6.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You make some comments here about someone called Stjepan Mestrovic. As a matter of fact, has he had access to your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Well, I certainly haven't sent him a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just tell us, in summary, what's contained here about him, in case it becomes of value later.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the interest of this, and this is why it's in an appendix rather than the main body of the report, the reason for drawing this material to the attention of the Court is to illustrate the kind of ways in which the discussion about the nature and relationship between ethnic groups in the region had tended to become focused. I wouldn't like this to be thought of as a comment on my part as saying that Stjepan Mestrovic is a racist, but it's an unfortunate consequence, I think, of the resurrection of the work of people like Tomasic, that they tend to lean in the direction of assuming that groups of people have permanent and indelible characteristics. That kind of discourse, I think, does point us in the direction of racist discourse.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Has the effect, as you suggest at the end of the first paragraph, as exploiting those who wish to find -- or leads to the potential exploitation by those who wish to find academic justification for extreme political views?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is one of the risks of any kind of academic work, that you have no control over how your work is received. I think this is probably true of Mestrovic as well, but I don't think he sets out to stimulate racist attitudes. But the way in which this work has been received and read -- it often happens. I mean, Samuel Huntington's work on the clash of civilisations has had a similar exploitation, similar misuse in the region by people trying to prove that there are necessary and inevitable conflicts between different ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can such views, for example, find a place in the thinking and works of somebody like Valenta?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would have thought so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's all I ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Allcock, for having come. You are released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will take 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You are Fuad Zeco, are you not, born in Breza on the 6th of July, 1932?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You graduated as a veterinarian, you worked as a veterinarian, and you are now retired.

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: After your veterinary studies, you were appointed, in 1968, as director of the veterinarian station of the Vitez municipality, were you not?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The zone of Vitez was a rural area and, as such, it had a large number of livestock.

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: During your veterinarian activities, you moved around a great deal and you met a lot of people, did you not?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You lived in Vitez, close to your place of work, the veterinarian centre, in a part of Vitez called Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The majority of the population of this area were Croat by nationality.

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Mr. Zeco, you were never engaged in politics in your life and you were never a member of any political party, were you?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: I should like to ask you to talk to us a little about the relations between the Croats and Muslims in Vitez. Those relations were good and harmonious, up to the point when the HVO was established in Vitez; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes, very good, the relations were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The period we are talking about when this change occurred is the spring of 1992.

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes. I was thinking of the period up to 1992 when relations were excellent, and after the appearance of the HVO in 1992, the relations started to change for the worse.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The HVO in Vitez, once established, little by little took over power; would you agree with that statement?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: The procedure that occurred following the emergence of the HVO was one that I could not accept, and the situation that developed was unacceptable to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You noted that the HVO started setting up patrols and checkpoints in the town and on the roads.

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: There were patrols within the territory of Vitez municipality, in the villages, and also in the town of Vitez itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The persons who were checked at these checkpoints were exclusively Muslims, were they not?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: The Muslims were those who were exclusively subject to checks and searches by members of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The HVO was able to identify people as Muslims. How did they know what ethnic group people belonged to when they checked them at these checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Well, these were more or less local people. They asked people to give their names, and if they were Muslim, they would be checked, interrogated, and so on. The people who were patrolling on the part of the HVO knew me well. I was well-known as a veterinarian in the area. So they all knew me and they knew who I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: So you yourself, you personally were the subject of control?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes, on a number of occasions. I was checked; I was asked where I was going, why I was going there. Though it was well-known why I had to pass, but still they checked me, asked me whether I was carrying a weapon, and what the purpose of my trip was, though it was quite clear that I was going to do my job.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: As regards the personnel working in municipal institutions, Mr. Zeco, would it be true to say that at a certain point in time in 1992, they were asked to sign a document recognising the power of the HVO, an act of loyalty towards the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: I was in close and frequent contact with representatives of the authorities. I also collaborated with those institutions so that I knew most of the people employed in the municipal bodies. I knew almost all of them, both Croats and Muslims. Among the people working in the municipal authorities was my wife, who worked in the cadastre of the municipality, and one day she came home very excited and disturbed, telling me that she had been asked to sign a document of loyalty to the newly formed municipal body, that is, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and if she failed to sign, she would be dismissed; she would lose her job. This happened to all the employees who were Muslims or of Bosniak nationality employed in the municipal bodies of authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You also told us that the Croatian flag, the flag of Herceg-Bosna had been hoisted at the municipality building.

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that well. I think it was in June 1992 when this flag was hoisted of the Croatian state and the flag of Herceg-Bosna. The same flag was raised at the building of the Secretariat of the Interior, known as the SUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regarding this particular question, can one conclude from the answer of the witness that there were two flags, the flag of the Herceg-Bosna community and the Croatian flag, the flag of the Croatian state?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Because of all these facts that you have just described to us, the Muslim community of Vitez and the leadership of the local Muslim intelligentsia started to organise themselves, and that is how a committee for the coordination of the protection of Muslim interests was established in July of 1992; is that correct, Mr. Zeco?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You yourself were appointed a member of this coordination committee in charge of the sector of agriculture, livestock production, and also civil defence matters because you had some training in civil defence.

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Certain members of that committee belonged to political parties and others did not, like yourself.

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Mr. Zeco, you knew somebody called Anto Valenta, who was an ideologue with considerable influence within the HVO, and you had discussions with this gentleman. Could you briefly report to us the substance of those discussions?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: I would frequently come across Mr. Anto Valenta. My wife, as I have just said, worked in the department for property and the cadastre; she's a surveyor by training. Frequently, when I went to the municipal building, I would drop in to see my wife, where I would also meet with Mr. Anto Valenta, who was looking for geographic maps in the cadastre. Since we knew each other, he even said to me, "Look, this is how we should deal with the question of maps, so that people belonging to one ethnic group should organise themselves and live as a people in a certain territory," and we had discussions along those lines. When I said, "What about life here in this area? We've all been living here together" but he kept insisting on his theory, explaining that each nation should live in a particular area and that that is how we should organise ourselves. In those days, I found this most surprising, and I was not pleased at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: This same gentleman, during those discussions, told you that, in his view, the Croats do not have sufficient positions of importance in the municipal government and that this should change.

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Exactly. That is what he said. He said that Croats up till then had not been adequately represented and did not have the influence that they should have; however, I didn't agree with him on that point, and we would have disputes over that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Anto Valenta appeared very regularly on Vitez, Busovaca, and Kiseljak television.

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes. Very, very frequently, he would be seen on the screens of local TV stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Also with him on the screen, there was often Ignac Kostroman, Tihomir Blaskic, and the accused, Dario Kordic.

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Did you know personally the family of the accused, Dario Kordic, and especially the father, Pero Kordic, who was a veterinarian, like you, but in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes. With Mr. Pero Kordic, Dario Kordic's father, I was a close friend and also his mother, Rozika. We were true friends and we frequently visited one another, especially on special festive occasions. I was a guest in their home frequently for Christmas and Easter, and Dario Kordic's parents were guests in my home during Bajram and other such festivities.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You personally were able to see that the Kordic family was an extremely religious family and that the father, Pero Kordic, was very active in religious organisations.

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The last time that you spoke to Dario Kordic's father, Pero Kordic, was in January 1993 when there was a conflict going on in the area of Busovaca, and you telephoned Dario Kordic's father. Could you tell us what Mr. Pero Kordic told you on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: I had a great deal of respect and appreciation for the religious feelings of my friend, Mr. Pero Kordic, and we were genuinely close friends, so that after the events in Busovaca in January 1993, shortly after that, out of curiosity, I called up my friend Pero on the phone and I asked him -- I remember it very well; it was a Saturday -- and I asked him, "Colleague Pero, what's new in Busovaca?" and his answer was, "All kinds of things. There's livestock, there's everything, but there are no Muslims." As a friend, I was truly shocked and surprised by this statement, and I said, "Pero, that is, indeed, regrettable, that you should say this to me as your friend, a Muslim, that you could say something like that to me," and since then, I never met or had any contact again with my friend, Pero Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: When you made that remark to your friend, Pero Kordic, what was his answer?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: He said that that was how things stood and that that was what it was like.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Now let us move on to another period, Mr. Zeco. We reached the month of October 1992, and in October 1992, you personally saw trucks and cars of HVO armed soldiers who were going in the direction of Novi Travnik, coming from Busovaca, and who were trying to pass through Vitez.

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: In that same period, you attended a meeting of the coordination committee for the protection of Muslims, and the local Muslim commander, Sefkija Dzidic, told you that the BiH army had decided to set up checkpoints in Ahmici and Stara Bila, to prevent the conflict spreading from Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The HVO issued an ultimatum for the removal of those checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Still within that same time frame, the HVO attacked the BH army headquarters in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes, it did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: This headquarters had to move, did it not, as a result?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes, it did. As the result of the attack by the HVO units, the headquarters of the army, which was located in the building of the secondary school centre, had to be moved to Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The logistics centre was also attacked at that time, was it not?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes, in the immediate vicinity of the army headquarters was where the logistics headquarters was located, in a private house, the centre of the army in Vitez. A very close associate of mine, Ahmic Cazim, was there, and the members of the HVO units physically attacked him, and they also launched an attack on that logistics headquarters belonging to the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: During the last week of this same month of October in 1992, Mr. Zeco, you, yourself, were physically attacked by a group of HVO soldiers wearing camouflage uniforms in the area of Krizancevo Selo, were you not?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes. Throughout that time, I did my professional duties, and I was called out to Krizancevo Selo to intervene professionally. On my return from Krizancevo Selo, at the entrance to the village, on the main road through Vitez, that part of the road is very narrow, and you could only have one vehicle moving in one direction. I was in my own vehicle moving along the road. Behind me there was another vehicle which was occupied by the members of the HVO units. They hit me and honked their horn and gave me signs to move aside so that they could pass. There was nothing I could do but to go on for 50 metres, because that was the narrow section of the road, so I went on driving my vehicle, and when I emerged from that section, I moved aside. But the vehicle with the HVO members, the HVO members got out of the car, and they opened my doors, one of the members of the HVO, and with his foot, with his leg, he attacked me physically, and he broke my -- the bone in my nose. At the same time, the other soldier -- because they already knew me; that is to say, they recognised me -- he grabbed hold of the soldier, because he had taken up a machine gun, and he said to me, "Doctor, flee from here." So I got back into my car and -- all bloody as I was; blood was still running out of my nose -- I fled to the police station in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You wanted to submit a complaint with the police, and you addressed the chief of police, Mr. Samir, and he told you that according to his information, the soldiers who attacked you belonged to a group called the Vitezovi; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes. When I came in front of the police station building, everybody knew me, more or less, and Mirko Samir happened to be there at the time. He was the chief of MUP, and I knew him. He asked me what had happened, and I told him what had happened, and he immediately said to me, "Well, wait here for a moment," and he sent his policemen off and told them -- he ordered them to go on the spot and to ascertain what had in fact happened. He personally took me -- he got into the car with me, my car with me, and we went to the first-aid station together, in Vitez, where I was given medical treatment. He insisted upon me going to the hospital in Travnik for a further medical examination in order to determine the objective state of my injuries. However, I said that I was going to go home and that I would think about it and see what I was going to do next. That's what I did do, in fact; I went home.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: So Mr. Samir told you that there was nothing he could do to follow up your complaint because these were military men, and in fact your complaint never was followed through?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: When I went home, about half an hour later, Mr. Samir Mirko, Mirko Samir, came with two policemen, he came to my house with them. In a way he apologised to me on that occasion and said that for the time being, he could do nothing because the circumstances were such, and he insisted that I go to Travnik and have a checkup so that we could have the results of that medical checkup, and when the time was ripe and the situation was favourable, he would then take steps, whereas for the time being, as they were military circumstances and military needs, there was nothing he could do about it, and that the situation was as it stood at the moment. In that way he sort of tried to apologise and calm me down and console me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You never learnt what happened with your complaint and any subsequent inquiries?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Quite by chance, one month later, a friend of mine who worked in the municipality of Vitez called me and said, "I've got something to show you." He took me off. In front of a building there was a pillar, and on the pillar was a death certificate stuck to it with -- an obituary notice, with a photograph on it, and he said, "This is the soldier who attacked you and who broke your nose." He said, "Well, you see, he's dead. He seems to have killed himself through adverse circumstances." I read this obituary notice. As far as I remember, his surname was Grabovac. Grabovac. That was the surname, as far as I can remember. He came from the area of Cajdras, the Zenica municipality. That's what I remember about all that. But, as I say, I didn't attach any particular importance to that. It was a fact, and I accepted it as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: As far as you know, that soldier was never punished for his attack on you?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: No. I only know that at that time, I was told that the policemen who went on the spot to ascertain the facts and circumstances had been given information that of those present, nobody must state who was present. This was something that Darko Kraljevic raised, who was in a cafe where the policeman had turned up, and they had been given orders that nobody was to betray the individual who had launched the attack on me. That's what I was told by the policemen who went on the spot to investigate in that particular case. That was the information that I got from those policemen who escorted Mirko Samir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: This Vitezovi unit was previously called HOS and joined the HVO in the summer of 1992; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Those were precisely those people referred to as HOS, the HOS unit. At its head was Darko Kraljevic, my neighbour, a close neighbour of mine, the son of Kraljevic, the father, who is a friend of mine, Stanko, and the mother of Darko Kraljevic worked with my wife, they were colleagues in the same office, so that I knew the family very well. I knew Darko's family very well. Darko and his younger brother went to school together with my own daughters, and I was the individual who --

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: This Vitezovi unit was stationed close to your house in the building of the forestry administration; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes. We are quite close. Everything was -- the forestry administration, my house, my veterinarian station, Darko's house, where I worked -- everything was within 300 square metres, a space of 300 square metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: In that same building, was there a unit of the Vitez Brigade that was stationed there?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: On the premises of the forestry administration building, it was the forestry administration building that we called the Sumarija in Rijeka, and in that particular building was where the headquarters, the command of the Rijeka unit was located, that particular unit of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Excuse me; the translation was "the command of Rijecko"; is that "Rijeka"? The name of the area, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Rijeka, and the adjective "Rijecka." Yes, the place was called Rijeka. Quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: In January of 1993, Mr. Zeco, you were a member of the war presidency which replaced the coordination committee for the protection of Muslims, and you were entrusted with the civil defence affairs for the Municipality of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes. In January, the war presidency was set up for the Vitez municipality, whose member I was, and I was appointed commander of the municipal headquarters of civil defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now go on to the month of April 1993. On the 16th of April, 1993, Mr. Zeco, you were at home when, around 5.30 in the morning, you heard the bombing of the town of Vitez, and you were not at all expecting an attack on the town?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Not at all. At least I, personally, did not, and the people who were in contact with me then, we had no intimation whatsoever that what took place on that 16th of April in the morning at 5.30 would happen. At 5.30 in the morning I was woken up, and so was my wife, by shooting and shelling. And after a short space of time -- that is to say, half an hour of that -- the members of HVO units came up to the house, and they asked me to open up.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Just a moment, please, Mr. Zeco. This attack on the town of Vitez, was it by the BH army or the HVO?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: No, it was not. At least I, myself, as a member of the war presidency, not at all. It was not any kind of sign that the army, BH army, did anything in the line of an armed attack on any kind of institutions or property or whatever. There was absolutely no sign of this, especially as on the 15th of April, there was a meeting of the war presidency at which the commander of the Armija, Dzidic Sefkija, was present, and I myself was at a joint meeting of the commission for the sowing season in the municipality, but I nonetheless succeeded in arriving at the meeting of the war presidency, towards its end, and the meeting was attended by the commander of the BH army, Sefkjia, and he didn't say at all that anything like that could happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The soldiers that appeared at your home on that morning, around 6.00, 6.30 in the morning, were they HVO soldiers or soldiers of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: No, they were soldiers of the HVO, and amongst them I recognised two. They were my neighbours, Krunoslav Bonic, nicknamed Kico, who came up to my door directly and said, "Doctor, put your clothes on, I have to take you off." And in the vicinity was the son of Zvonko Karin, my neighbour, his son, I don't know his name, but he was there too, and they told me to get dressed because they were going to take me off to a certain place.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Mr. Zeco, didn't you know the name of Krunoslav Bonic?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes, I did, but he's a younger generation from me. I don't remember exactly, but I did know --

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: I'm asking you for the first name of the father of Krunoslav Bonic, the father, the first name.

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes, I knew the father well, Krunoslav Bonic's father.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Just his name.

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Franjo, Franjo Bonic was his name. By profession he is a waiter, and so --

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. This Krunoslav Bonic who arrested you, did you know whether he was captured by the BH army during the conflict and where he now lives?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes, he was captured. After the war conflict ceased, he was arrested. I know that he was arrested and that he spent his time in prison in Travnik, and after that, after a certain amount of time spent in prison, he moved to Australia. That's what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: I'm going to show you a photograph, Mr. Zeco, reference number Z2764. Mr. Zeco, can you tell me whether you recognise on this photograph Krunoslav Bonic that you have been telling us about?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Thank you. After being arrested, Mr. Zeco, in your home, and then you were taken to the veterinary station where you used to work, and you noted upon your arrival that some 50 Muslim detainees were already in the basement of that building; is that so?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes. They took me to the veterinary station, and in the basement of that building, in the office premises and the halls where we examined the animals, there were already about 40 individuals there, exclusively of Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: I'm now going to show you a photograph, Mr. Zeco, the reference number 2765. This photograph, does it show the veterinary station you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes. You can see the veterinary station building, the one that I have just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to show you another document, Mr. Zeco, which is an aerial photograph of the neighbourhood in Vitez called Rijeka. It is marked Z1971. This is a document which was annexed, attached to your statement of 1997, and at the time, you explained to the investigator where the various buildings were located, the various institutions we have mentioned so far. Can you confirm to us that this document does, indeed, show the headquarters in Rijeka, the veterinarian station in which you were detained together with other Muslims, and then finally on the right-hand side, shows where your own house is located?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes, quite so. That is precisely the photograph of the locality called Rijeka. I can see the veterinarian station building here, I can see my own house, I can see the Sumarija, and I recognise ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Could you show where your house was, Mr. Zeco, on the video or on the screen, where the headquarters were, where Sumarija was, and where the station was where you worked?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: That is the veterinarian station [indicating]. This is my own house [indicating]. This is the veterinarian station [indicating]. This is my own house [indicating]. That's right. This part here [indicating], that is the forestry administration building called Sumarija.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Mr. Zeco, and it is in that building, the forestry administration building, that there were the Vitezovi on the one hand and the headquarters of the unit of the Vitez Brigade in Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The three locations are very close to one another, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: I said a moment ago that the area is 300 square metres in size. It's one next to each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: We no longer need the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: In the cellar of that veterinarian station, there were other prisoners from the neighbourhood of Rijeka, and they were detained there too, bringing the number to some 70 people.

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes. All the prisoners more or less who were detained there, there were about 70 to 76 people -- at one point, there were 76, I know that -- they were called out and taken away. But for the most part, there were about 70 people, mostly Muslims from the local community of Rijeka. However, there were a few people from another area of Vitez. Mostly, they were Muslims who had been caught there during the attack, who had been in the Rijeka area during the attack, and as they were Muslims, they were arrested and taken to the building and held prisoner there in the building of the veterinarian station. There were maybe five or six individuals from another area, not from the Rijeka local community area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Were all the detainees civilians?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: They were exclusively civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: All males?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Male, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You were detained there together with that group of people for four days, after which you were taken to the Dubravica school, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes, we were all detained there at the veterinarian station, and on the fourth day, we were transferred from the veterinarian station, we were transferred to -- we went from in front of the Sumarija building, buses came to pick us up, and we were then transferred to the school which was in the Dubravica area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Before we come to speak about that transfer, I'd like you to tell us how things developed at the station. The guards there did not provide you with any food, did they, but your families were authorised to take food and drinks to you; is that so?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes. Our families, who lived more or less close by, would come and bring us food. There were no problems at that time for food to be brought to us and given to us. So as far as the food question was concerned for the people there, it was just that people who lived outside the Rijeka area, they were helped too by the families of the detainees from the area, so that these others would also be given food by the families of the detainees.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: In respect of the guards at this centre, at this station, you noticed that they would regularly come in in order to select detainees and for the detainees to go and dig trenches in the Rijeka and Kruscica areas.

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes. Throughout the time spent at the veterinarian station, soldiers would come, several soldiers would arrive, and they would ask the person in charge of us, the one who was the organiser of the people detained at the veterinarian station, they asked him for a certain number of prisoners, to take them off, and we know from the stories told by the people when they returned that they were taken to dig trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The commander of the veterinarian station, which was then used as a detention centre, was, indeed, Zeljko Matkovic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes, he was the commander of the prisoners being held at the veterinarian station. He was in command, Zeljko Matkovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: He was from Rijeka. You knew him; is that so?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: I knew him very well. He was a teacher by profession, and he lived close by. He was a neighbour, so I knew him very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: During those four days, some of the people that had been selected to go and dig trenches were killed. Among them, Jusuf Ibrakovic and Mr. Nesib Hurem; is that so?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes. When they had been -- when a group had been taken away, upon their return, when they came back from trench-digging, they said that on the occasion, Jusuf Ibrakovic, called Juso, was killed -- had been killed. I got to know him and I was interested in this because he did not come from the Rijeka area, but he was from the area of Stari Vitez. At that particular time, his mother phoned me up and asked me --

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Excuse me. Unfortunately, it may not be necessary to mention all the details. I just wanted to show you two documents. These are death certificates with regard to Mr. Jusuf Ibrakovic and Mr. Nesib Hurem. Their numbers are Z22104 and Z22105. Mr. Zeco, could you please tell us whether these death certificates do represent Mr. Ibrakovic and Mr. Hurem, whom you've just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, precisely so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Lopez-Terres, I'd like to find out if the witness himself was selected for trench-digging; if not, if he's able to offer any explanation as to the method of selecting people for trench-digging.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Can you please answer the Judge's question, Mr. Zeco?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes. The HVO soldiers would come to the building of the veterinarian station, and they would ask Zeljko Matkovic to supply them with 10 to 15 prisoners so that they could take them off. They asked for physically stronger men. So he would select -- how he selected this was left to him, and he would select these individuals which he would then send off with the soldiers to do trench-digging.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You didn't quite answer the first question, Mr. Zeco. Were you yourself forced to go and dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: No. No, they didn't take me off to dig trenches. Nobody asked me to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The sides where the trenches were dug were in close vicinity to the confrontation line, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: The prisoners at the veterinarian station, they took them off to the confrontation line, to the Kruscica area. That was the area they were taken to to dig trenches; that is to say, the prisoners from the veterinarian station.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Are you aware of the circumstances under which Mr. Hurem and Mr. Ibrakovic were killed?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Jusuf Ibrakovic, according to the stories told by the rest, the other people who went to dig trenches, tried to take an automatic rifle which was in front of him. How the rifle came to be in front of him -- when he took the rifle, one of the soldiers who was there close by shot at him directly, and he killed Jusuf Ibrakovic; whereas Nesib Hurem, he died while he was digging trenches; he died from a bullet fired from some area. Nobody said where the shot came from or how this happened, but he was killed during trench-digging. That was the information that I got.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: During the time that you spent in the detention centre, the HVO soldiers took your car, didn't they, and the car was never returned to you later on, was it?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. They asked me to give them the keys. The keys were in my pocket; they took the keys. The garage was in the immediate vicinity. They took the vehicle off, and I know because I saw from the veterinarian station. I could see it in the courtyard of the forestry administration building. After that, I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: It is in that vehicle that a plan for the protection and evacuation of Muslim civilians was found. You had prepared that plan in case there was an attack by the HVO; is that so?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes, in the car. As it was my duty to prepare a plan for the safeguarding and protection of Muslim citizens in case of an HVO attack, I said a moment ago that I went to a meeting of the war presidency, and I was given the assignment of preparing, for the meeting of the 16th of April, a plan of this kind and to present them a plan for the safeguarding and protection of the Muslim people in case of an HVO attack. That plan was precisely in my car in a cassette, and the HVO soldiers -- because later on, for a brief period, Zeljko Matkovic told me about this plan that was found, that was discovered, and they said that it was allegedly a war plan, but it wasn't. It was just a plan to safeguard and protect the civilians and property in case of an HVO attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Still whilst you were being detained in the veterinarian station, on the 18th of April, 1993, two days following your arrival there, Zeljko Matkovic, whom you've just mentioned, asked you and the other detainees, he told you to go to the cellar of the veterinarian station. Do you remember the words he said to you then?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes. He expressly ordered -- he said that everybody who was in the offices, in the examination hall, in the hallway, corridors, because the space was restricted, he asked us all to go down to the basement, and some 70 of us all went down. He said, "Something is going to happen. What will happen will be seen, but you all have to go to the basement," and that's what we did. After a short period of time there, an explosion was heard, and Zeljko Matkovic finally came and said, "You can come out now. Now you know. With this, the question has been solved of the Muslims in the Vitez area." We still did not know anything. We just knew that we heard an explosion, detonation. What it was, later on, we learnt that it was an explosion in Stari Vitez of explosives there that were activated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Can you tell us more about the explosion? What do you know about it? What was explained to you as to the cause of the explosion?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: I did not understand the question fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Sir, there was an explosion on the 18th of April, 1993. Could you tell us what it was actually?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've got his evidence about that, Mr. Lopez-Terres, and we, of course, have heard other evidence. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Four days after you had arrived at the station, you were transferred to the Dubravica school. You explained to us that you first went to the Sumarija building where buses were waiting for you; is that so?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: This school --

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: -- in front of the Sumarija administration building.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: How far was the Dubravica school from the veterinarian station?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Well, the distance is about a kilometre away, as the crow flies, I mean. Perhaps it's 1.200 or 1.300 metres. That is the distance from the forestry administration building to the school in Dubravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: In the building of the forestry administration, a unit of the Vitez Brigade was stationed, and it was headed by somebody you knew. Could you give us the name of that commander?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes, the commander of that unit at Rijeka was Karlo Grabovac, whom I knew personally, and I know that he was the commander of the unit at Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Do you know his father's first name?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes. I know the whole family. There is Jozo Grabovac, who worked at the post office.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Thank you. How old, approximately, was Karlo Grabovac?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Well, he was between 50 and 55 years of age at the time; that is to say, I'm speaking about the 1993 period.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: I mean Karlo Grabovac's age; I wanted to know how old the son was.

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Karlo was between 23 and 25 years of age, somewhere thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: As far as you know, was Karlo Grabovac the superior in the chain of command to Zeljko Matkovic?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And he was in charge of the areas of Kruscica and Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I think that the command of that unit for the Kruscica area in Vitez was in the forestry administration building, and all the orders which were issued to Zeljko Matkovic would come from the forestry administration building, the orders which he executed and which he acted upon. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: As far as you know, was the accused, Mario Cerkez, Karlo Grabovac's commander?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes, I know that. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: As far as you know, there were several centres in Vitez, weren't there, in which there were units of the Vitez Brigade. You mentioned five centres in addition to the main centre where the headquarters was.

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: I think that touring the Vitez municipality region, I came to realise that in certain localities, there were certain commands of those military units, and I knew that there was the Rijeka unit, the Dubravica one, the Stara Bila one, in Kruscica, Divjak. All those were commands in command of the HVO units in the Vitez municipality. The main command, the headquarters of the Vitez municipality, was in town in the cultural centre, that is to say, in the hotel building. For the Vitez municipality, that was the headquarters, the sort of supreme headquarters for all the other headquarters in the Vitez area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: This supreme headquarters was in the hands of Mario Cerkez; is that so?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: When you were transferred to the Dubravica school, you were put together with the other detainees in the gym premises, and you noticed that there were already other people detained there, women, children, and some men, coming from the region of Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that well. When we arrived, as you have just described it, that was the situation I came across when we arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Were you able to gauge the number of prisoners that were together with you in that gym premises?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: About that number, there were about that many people there, because during our detention on the premises, we had to solve the question of food. So we would assess the situation and we had to count the number of people there, and we found that there were about 360 detainees there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Whilst you were being detained at the Dubravica school, you were authorised to receive drinks and food from your families, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes. We were brought food by the members of the HVO. They would bring in food that our families had brought to the courtyard of the forestry administration building. Then they would take over this food brought by our families, and they were told when to bring that food, so that they could then take it to us, to the Dubravica school. During our detention at the Dubravica school, we would get this food regularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: During your detention, you received staple products, such as soap, underwear, clean underwear, that sort of thing, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, the people that brought us the food, we would tell them what else we would like to have brought to us. They would then convey our wishes, and we would get underwear or whatever we required in the way of personal items. So this was solved, fully solved, this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Among the male detainees in the Dubravica school, were some of them selected for trench-digging, and were they taken to specific areas which you could mention for us?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. During the time we spent in Dubravica, there would be demands from the HVO -- more demand from the HVO, so that prisoners would be taken off for trench-digging more and more. They were usually taken to the area of Nadioci, Pirici, Kuber, Sivrino Selo, Tolovici. For the most part, those were the areas where there were some front lines in the area. So throughout the time we spent in the camp, prisoners were taken off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lopez-Terres, it's now the time to adjourn. Is that a convenient moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Half past two. Mr. Zeco, we're going to adjourn until half past two. Would you please be back then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Would you remember not to speak to anybody about your evidence during this and any other adjournment, and that includes the members --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- of the Prosecution? Thank you very much. Half past two. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.02 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lopez-Terres.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Mr. Zeco, before the break, you told us the various places where the prisoners were taken to dig trenches from the school in Dubravica. You testified as a witness in the General Blaskic case in September 1997, and at the time, you marked a document representing various geographical zones, and I'm going to show you a copy of that document now, which was marked 29 in the Blaskic case and will have our reference Z2767. Would you look at that document, Mr. Zeco, and confirm that this is indeed a copy of the document on which you testified in September 1997, and would you again indicate the various places where prisoners were taken to dig trenches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are getting the French translation. Mr. Lopez-Terres, the spots have been marked on this plan; there's no need for the witness to do it again. We will simply accept the plan. Mr. Zeco, there is no need to go over it again. Are the places which you marked on here the places at which trenches had to be dug?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. These little arrows here indicate the places where the prisoners were digging trenches, and they are in the northeastern part of the Vitez municipality: Tolovici, Vrhovine, Pirici --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Zeco, let me interrupt; we can see from the plan. If anybody wants to ask you any questions about it, they can. Yes, can we go on, please, Mr. Lopez-Terres.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Mr. Zeco, as far as you remember, some of the detainees who went to dig trenches in the areas we have referred to, were they killed or wounded during this forced labour?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes. There were some who were killed, some of the detainees, and there were some who were wounded, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You were kept informed at the school in Dubravica of the fate of those who went to dig trenches, and upon their return to the school, they told you of what had happened, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: During these reports made to you by the prisoners, they told you that they were forced to dig trenches and that very frequently they were mistreated, physically and psychologically, and also humiliated; is that true?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Could you also confirm the story of what one of the prisoners told you regarding what happened in the area of Nadioci?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes. Let me mention quite a drastic example of this psychological and physical abuse. A young prisoner who was under 20 -- I know him well; he used to work in a tyre repair shop -- became physically and psychologically broken. He told us the story that members of the HVO had mistreated them in such a way that they tied a pig to a tree, and they forced him to have intercourse with that pig. However, this didn't happen. Even though he had agreed to do it, they gave up the idea, but this had a terrible effect on him and the others who were present.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: I should now like to show the Chamber a video clip of a film taken in this Dubravica school in April 1993. It is Prosecution Exhibit 1625-1.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we play the tape, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are several extracts.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Black Legion" is written.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I think we can stop there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Mr. Zeco, you've seen these several abstracts. This film was shot in the areas of the school at Dubravica. Did you recognise the halls of that school?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I recognised the school, and I even saw the spot where I was detained.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: That was in the gym, wasn't it, the Sports Hall?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: On the screen, at a given moment, we saw a drawing on the wall with the words "Crna Legija." Could you tell us what that means?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: It was the emblem of the Vitezovi, as far as I was informed, and they were headed by Darko Kraljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Thank you. When you were with the other detainees in this school of which we just saw some pictures, you were informed by the guards at that school that should the BH army attack the institution, it would be totally destroyed by explosives and also by setting alight the petrol tank that was to be found in the school; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: At the time we arrived, and that was in the period from the 19th to the 21st of April, I think, in the immediate vicinity of the school, where we were held, there was shooting. There was a battle going on, and the shooting came quite close to the school at one point, and it was then that HVO soldiers came and told us that the ground around the school was mined, and that should the army attack, that we would be blown up together with the building; that is, that in the basement there was a fuel tank, and that it would be set alight. That is what we were told.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Were you then told by the local commander that indeed, the HVO had confirmed this, that should the offensive continue, the building would be destroyed by explosives, together with the detainees in it?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes. Later on, after some time, when I left the area of Vitez municipality and crossed into territory under control of the BH army, I had a direct contact with the commander of an army brigade in the area of Vitez, that is commander Mensud Kelestura, who told me that the HVO had said that should the army continue its offensive, they would blow up the building together with the Muslim detainees in that building at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You were eventually released, together with the other detainees, on the 30th of April, 1993, but before being able to go home, you were asked whether you and the other detainees wanted to stay in Vitez or to leave the region.

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes. We were told that we should all go to an office where things had already been prepared and tell them what we wanted to do, whether we wanted to stay in Vitez or to leave the area of Vitez. I personally expressed the wish to stay in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The office that you mentioned that had been prepared, were there only soldiers inside or also civilians who were among those who put these questions to you?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: There were soldiers in there, but the administrative matters were mostly dealt with by certain women in civilian clothes. They were administrative employees there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The prisoners who came from Ahmici were taken by bus to Zenica upon their release, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: They couldn't return to their homes.

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: No. We were told that the prisoners from Ahmici would be taken by bus and relocated to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: They didn't have a choice, I think.

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: During the night of the 2nd of May, 1993, a few days later when you were at home, two HVO soldiers appeared at your house and started searching it. Could you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: After my release and return to my home, the second night, two soldiers came, HVO soldiers, who said that they had received a report that there was a radio transmitter in my house and that they wanted to search the house to check. They went through the whole house, they searched it, and said, "It's okay," and they left the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Was Krunoslav Bonic one of the two soldiers, the one who you mentioned this morning?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: After leaving your house, these two soldiers came back, in fact, half an hour later and took you to a house in the area of Sofa, after putting handcuffs on you.

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes. About half an hour later, a group of soldiers, I think three or four of them, came. Because there were other soldiers behind them, I didn't turn around to look, they were masked, with something over their heads, they took me to a room in the area of Sofa, to a small hut, and they took me inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Excuse me for intervening. It must be a matter of translation. "Sofa" is a region of Vitez, a geographic area, not a sofa, as such, as a piece of furniture.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: There's a place called Sofa; that's what the people of Vitez call it?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes, it is just behind my house or, rather, just behind the veterinarian station, maybe 200 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You noted traces of blood on the walls in that house. What else did you note?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes. When I entered this room, I was really -- I don't know how to say -- extremely astonished because I saw on the walls splashes of blood, and inside there was a pile of beer cans, and I became apprehensive of my own fate.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: While going to that house, you were hit several times, including by the soldier Bonic.

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes. Among the others who were there, they were masked, they had a cover over their faces, but I recognised by his voice and face and general appearance that Bonic was one of them. They even physically abused me. They told me to lie down and that I mustn't turn around. I moved a little bit and peeked behind, when one of them hit me with his pistol butt, and shortly after that, they fired a shot just above my head so that this warm air hit me, and I thought I had been shot, that I had been hit; fortunately, I hadn't. But one of the consequences is that I had this ringing sound in my ears, and ever since then, I have problems with my hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: While you were in the house, the same soldiers brought in another prisoner whom you recognised as Mr. Midhat Hodzic, the former mayor of the municipality, and who suffered the same fate as you, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes. About half an hour after my arrival, they brought in Midhat Hodzic, my neighbour, the former president of the municipality. They brought him into the same room in which I was, and they treated him in the same way as they had treated me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Those soldiers put questions to you. Did they interrogate you? Did they ask for information about the BH army, about the weapons that Muslims may have?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes. They gave us a piece of paper to write down, as far as we knew, where the BH army units were located, to tell them who were the men who had assisted in the procurement of weapons, which weapons were kept where, but both Midhat Hodzic and myself had no knowledge about these things that they were interested in. However, they kept insisting that we do that, and they were probably not satisfied with our replies and what we wrote down on this paper, and then they physically pressured us so that they hit us repeatedly and injured us physically.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: When, fortunately, they took you back home that night, these soldiers took a sum of 480 Deutschemarks that you had at home, and they ordered you to leave your house the next day at 5.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes, they told me that after 5.00, I must not be found in my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You stayed, nevertheless, and you went to the police station to submit a complaint regarding the suffering and the maltreatment and the order that you had received to leave the area, and you understood that that claim had little chance of producing any result.

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes. I asked the police to intervene, and I wanted to tell them what had happened. Two policemen came to my house, they drew up a report about the event, and I explicitly required their opinion and their view regarding my continued stay there, whether I should stay on or not. I asked them to go to the headquarters in the forestry administration building at Rijeka to convey this position that I should stay, and they promised to do that. But when they left, I saw that they didn't go to the headquarters, but rather that they went directly to their police station. So my conclusion was that they would not carry out the promise they had made to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: This headquarters you're referring to is the building of the Sumarija, where Mr. Grabovac was in command, the building you have already referred to?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Finally, you were taken in by a Croatian friend.

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes. In the meantime, a friend of mine came -- rather, a colleague of my wife's, his name was Zvonko Santic, he came to visit us because he had learnt that I had been released from prison. But when he heard what had happened that night, he himself said that if that was so, he would take us in and take us to his own house and provide protection for me and my wife in that way, which he did, indeed. We got into the car that he had come in and moved to the house of this friend of ours called Zvonko Santic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The next day, you tried to collect some personal belongings from your house and you noted that it was occupied.

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes. The next day, my wife -- because we hadn't prepared ourselves for moving, so the next day, my wife and Zvonko Santic drove us to my house to collect some personal belongings; however, when they arrived, they were prevented from entering the house or taking anything from it. However, Zvonko Santic intervened; he tried to explain that it was necessary, but the person who had already moved into the house called the HVO soldiers to intervene, and they again came from the Sumarija building, and they didn't allow them to go in but rather demanded that they leave, which they did, and came back without having completed what they set out to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: So you stayed with that Croatian family for several days, and on the 8th of May, 1993, soldiers of the military police of the HVO came to take you to the Vitez Hotel?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes. I was taken by military policemen, this time to the Vitez Hotel, to a room, and somebody I did not know was there. He must have had some sort of a position; he was wearing a camouflage uniform. He asked me what were the plans that I had compiled? I said that they were plans for the protection of the civilian population because I was the commander of the municipal civil defence staff, and these were exclusively plans to protect civilians, civilian property, in the case of war operations or conflicts. That was the plan for this. After a certain period of time and thinking things over, he said, "All right." He called a soldier and said to him, "This is the job of the civilian police," and that I should be taken to the police station, which I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: So you were then taken to the civilian police, who interrogated you again, and they held you for 48 hours?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes. I was taken to the police station. They drew up a report about everything. After compiling this report, which I signed, I was taken to a room which had a toilet and an improvised bed and a blanket, and I spent 48 hours there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You were then released and told to stay under house arrest for a while?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO
utterances.text: Yes.
